dialogue.about: like part 1: a booking call with a spelled name, a phone number and a price

turns.speaker: staff
turns.text: Good morning, Harbour Bike Tours. How can I help you?

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Oh, hello. I'm calling about the guided rides you run at the weekends. A friend of mine did one last month and said it was the best way to see the coast.

turns.speaker: staff
turns.text: That's lovely to hear. We have two rides on Saturdays: a short one along the river, which takes about two hours, and the longer coastal ride, which is closer to five hours with a stop for lunch.

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: I think the coastal one. Is lunch included in the price?

turns.speaker: staff
turns.text: It is, yes. The coastal ride is £45.50 per person, and that covers the bike, a helmet and lunch at a café in the old fishing village. Can I take your name?

turns.speaker: caller
turns.text: Sure. It's Daniel Fairbrook. That's F-A-I-R-B-R-O-O-K.

turns.speaker: staff
turns.text: Thank you, Mr Fairbrook. And a contact number?

turns.speaker: staff
turns.text: Lovely. Now, we meet outside the station at half past eight, so please don't be late, because the group leaves on time. Oh, and if it's raining heavily, we'll text you by seven to let you know whether the ride is going ahead.

turns.speaker: staff
turns.text: Just a water bottle and a light jacket. The wind on the cliffs can be surprisingly cold, even in July.

lecture.about: like part 4: one speaker on an academic subject

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: Today I want to look at something most of us never notice: the street light. Before the nineteenth century, city streets after dark were lit, if at all, by candles or oil lamps hung outside houses, and in many towns householders were actually required by law to provide them.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: The arrival of gas lighting changed that completely. From the eighteen-twenties onwards, gas companies laid pipes under the main streets of large cities, and lamplighters walked their routes every evening with long poles, lighting each lamp by hand. Electric lighting followed at the end of the century, but it's worth remembering that gas lamps survived in some districts for decades, partly because the existing network was cheap to run.

turns.speaker: lecturer
turns.text: What interests historians is not only the technology, but the effect on daily life. Shops could stay open later, evening classes became possible for working people, and the sense of the street as a public space at night began to change. In the second half of this lecture, I'll look at the newest stage of the story: the switch to LED lights, and the debate about whether our cities are now too bright.
